source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)

coverage.syllabus: Lubbers IV.C Rulemaking: regulatory analysis pp. 324–344; Sunstein v. Heinzerling/Ackerman 325–329; Michigan v EPA 332; Corrosion Proof Fittings 335; problem 343
coverage.historicalCaveat: Executive order thresholds and casebook pre-2016 TSCA case discussed as textbook historical context; no implication of independently verified present-day 2026 status

topics.title: § 5.8 / § 5.8.1 — Cost-Benefit Analysis: Sunstein vs Heinzerling/Ackerman (pp. 324–330)
topics.description: Concept, systematic approach, numerical textbook illustrations, expected-value, statistical life, discounting, distributional and critique.

entries.title: Regulatory analysis: systematic estimate of policy impacts
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Formal regulatory analysis examines costs, benefits, alternatives and assumptions beyond conventional § 553 notice/comment; CBA monetizes effects when plausible.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency tries to see if a safety rule helps society enough compared with what it costs.
entries.legalExplanation: A structured analytic method often required by executive oversight and sometimes statutes; not inherently required of all rulemaking under APA § 553.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish source mandating analysis, what metrics, and judicial review route.
entries.examTrap: Not every public safety regulation must satisfy strict monetized benefits-over-costs threshold.

entries.title: CBA calculation framework
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Benefits = health/safety and other gains, sometimes monetized as expected adverse outcomes avoided × value per outcome plus other benefits; net benefits = benefits minus costs; benefit-cost ratio = benefits ÷ costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Add what society gains in dollar terms, subtract what rule costs, then evaluate tradeoffs.
entries.legalExplanation: Sunstein discusses quantitative ranges, willingness to pay, qualitative impacts and prioritization; uncertainty should be described, not hidden.
entries.examApplication: When exam presents numbers, state units and time horizon: dollars/year versus present value cannot be compared directly.
entries.examTrap: Counting only numbers can omit hard-to-measure harms and distributional impacts.

entries.title: Textbook worked example: 80 lives × $6 million
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Illustrative benefit = 80 × $6m = $480m; a rule with $200m estimated cost has net benefit +$280m (on equal scope/horizon).
entries.laymanExplanation: Saving 80 statistical lives at chosen $6m value is $480m of estimated benefit.
entries.legalExplanation: Sunstein's example is pedagogical, not official 2026 VSL or agency legal requirement.
entries.examApplication: Compute explicitly: 80 × 6 = 480; 480 - 200 = +280 (millions).

entries.title: Textbook worked example: 4 lives × $6 million
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Illustrative benefit = 4 × $6m = $24m; $400m rule would show net cost of $376m, before other benefits/values.
entries.laymanExplanation: The projected benefits are far below costs on the simple comparison.
entries.legalExplanation: Sunstein treats as usually not justified, while allowing explanation for special circumstances and unmonetized values.
entries.examApplication: Compute: 4 × 6 = 24; 24 - 400 = -376 (millions).

entries.title: Textbook willingness-to-pay range example
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: If each statistical life valued $3–8m, 20 avoided fatalities imply $60–160m of benefits; plus $40m other benefits = $100–200m; if rule costs $200m, net range -$100m to $0.
entries.laymanExplanation: Uncertain value gives range, not a single invented number.
entries.legalExplanation: Book uses historic $3–8m illustrative values; does not necessarily show all societal concerns captured.
entries.examTrap: Do not use these historical values as actual current EPA valuation without verification.

entries.title: Ranges and nonmonetized outcomes
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: When science uncertain, present low/high expected lives saved and avoid false numerical precision; quantify what can be quantified, state omitted effects.
entries.laymanExplanation: Better to say roughly 100–240 lives than invent exact 173.
entries.legalExplanation: Sunstein still supports agency qualitative explanation if monetization incomplete.
entries.examApplication: In exam make assumptions explicit and identify nonquantifiable benefits.

entries.title: Sunstein pro-CBA: opportunity costs and cooling effect
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: CBA helps allocate finite resources, counter emotional cognitive distortions and expose false alarms, while allowing concern for children, poor or involuntary exposure to outweigh arithmetic in exceptional cases.
entries.laymanExplanation: Choosing a costly rule means not spending same money to address another hazard; numbers can reveal opportunity costs.
entries.legalExplanation: Sunstein argues democratic value from transparent comparisons and bounded exceptions; CBA should not be arithmetic straightjacket.
entries.examApplication: State strongest pro side before critiques.
entries.examTrap: Do not portray Sunstein as requiring zero flexibility or literal strict formula.

entries.title: Heinzerling and Ackerman anti-CBA: lives not interchangeable dollars
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: CBA arguably conflates mortality risk with death, personal purchases with public protection, and cannot measure ecological and moral value objectively.
entries.laymanExplanation: A parent's safety or endangered species cannot necessarily be priced like a used car.
entries.legalExplanation: Authors question legitimacy of WTP, lack of science, and substituting pseudo-precise cost totals for substantive protection decisions.
entries.examApplication: Identify valuation assumptions and individual versus collective rights.
entries.examTrap: Critique does not imply agencies must ignore compliance cost when statute explicitly requires it.

entries.title: Distributional inequality and WTP wealth bias
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Willingness-to-pay measures ability as well as desire to pay; poor communities may register low financial values despite serious injury, and monetized aggregate CBA may hide who bears costs.
entries.laymanExplanation: If poor household can't afford to spend to avoid pollution, that doesn't mean its health worth less.
entries.legalExplanation: Heinzerling/Ackerman urge equity and environmental justice as independent considerations.
entries.examApplication: Discuss distributive effects even when aggregate net benefit positive.
entries.examTrap: Aggregate net benefits can mask concentrated injustice.

entries.title: Discounting future harms and benefits
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Discounting makes future outcomes worth less today; environmental critics fear diminishing delayed cancer and intergenerational harms, proponents use time value and life-years rationale.
entries.laymanExplanation: Preventing harm in 30 years may receive smaller present-dollar weight than harm tomorrow.
entries.legalExplanation: Discounting involves selected rate, timing of benefit, consistency of treatment; controversial with health and environment.
entries.examApplication: If given benefit B at year t and discount r, PV = B/(1+r)^t; specify time units.
entries.examTrap: Avoid discounting costs but not benefits or vice versa without reasons.

entries.title: Regulatory expertise, transparency and capture
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: CBA can expose assumptions, but complex expert-driven analyses may exclude lay people and make industry-favored assumptions appear objective.
entries.laymanExplanation: A giant spreadsheet can clarify tradeoffs or become a black box only insiders understand.
entries.legalExplanation: Heinzerling/Ackerman cite examples of perverse valuation, including avoided future pension payments from smoking mortality and parents' time buckling car seats.
entries.examApplication: Explain methodological dispute rather than asserting all CBA worthless.
entries.examTrap: Statutory law remains controlling regardless who wins policy debate.

topics.title: § 5.8.1 — Federal CBA Law: Executive Orders, Statutes and Review (pp. 330–335)
topics.description: EO 12866/14094 as textbook historical snapshot, organic statutes, Michigan v EPA, Cotton Dust, Entergy, NEPA/RFA and CAFE problem.

entries.title: EO 12866: significant executive-branch regulation and economic threshold
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Textbook recounts EO 12866 and OIRA oversight: executive agencies prepare more extensive economic analyses for significant rules (historically $100m/year; Biden EO 14094 raised figure to $200m in 2023).
entries.laymanExplanation: Very expensive federal rules usually get extra review; smaller rules may not.
entries.legalExplanation: Source values reflect textbook historical period and may have changed by 2026; judicial enforcement limited by order text.
entries.examApplication: State applicable time/version explicitly; distinguish statute from executive oversight.
entries.examTrap: Don't describe $200m as definitely current 2026 law absent present verification.

entries.title: Cost-benefit decisional language of EO 12866
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Order recommends regulations only upon reasoned finding benefits justify costs, recognizing unquantifiable effects; stronger EO 12291 preference for benefits exceeding costs illustrates spectrum.
entries.laymanExplanation: Try to choose policy worth its tradeoffs, but don't pretend every value has a price.
entries.legalExplanation: EO 12866 applies 'to extent permitted by law' and supports broader equity (2023 EO 14094) in historical textbook snapshot.
entries.examApplication: Contrast procedural duty to prepare analysis with substantive requirement to choose positive net benefits.
entries.examTrap: Executive order cannot override clear statute.

entries.title: Organic statutory mandates govern if CBA allowed or forbidden
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Cost assessment is required or permissible based on specific enabling statute; statutes using 'maximum feasible' or 'appropriate and necessary' may demand different tradeoffs.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency can't replace Congress's test with its own spreadsheet.
entries.legalExplanation: Clean Air, OSH Act and other statutes vary; congressional command controls, not OIRA preference.
entries.examApplication: Quote statutory words and interpret scope before testing analyses.
entries.examTrap: 'Feasible' does not automatically equal maximized net economic benefits.

entries.title: Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743 (2015)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: EPA deemed mercury controls 'appropriate and necessary' without considering costs at threshold; Court required cost consideration but not formal fully monetized CBA.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before calling stringent mercury regulation appropriate, agency had to account for what compliance costs.
entries.legalExplanation: Court held statute's phrase irrationally read to ignore cost; agency could choose how to consider it reasonably; dissent argued cost considered later.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish some cost consideration from full CBA mandate.
entries.examTrap: The casebook summarizes opinion rather than reproduces full merits reasoning.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in casebook Notes; full court opinion not reproduced

entries.title: American Textile Manufacturers Institute v. Donovan (Cotton Dust), 452 U.S. 490 (1981)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: OSHA 'to extent feasible' worker protection standard requires technological/economic feasibility, not cost-benefit maximization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Protect workers as much as doable, even if costs exceed monetized benefits.
entries.legalExplanation: Organic statute's feasible command overrides executive cost instructions.
entries.examApplication: Contrast Michigan and Entergy.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in casebook Notes; full court opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Entergy Corp. v. Riverkeeper, Inc., 556 U.S. 208 (2009)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Clean Water Act best-technology language could accommodate CBA in textbook under then-prevailing Chevron approach.
entries.laymanExplanation: Choosing 'best' can include economic efficiency if statute allows.
entries.legalExplanation: Book notes pre-Loper Chevron deference and uncertainty post-Chevron; legal meaning reviewed under current doctrine elsewhere in course.
entries.examApplication: Explain historical deference change, do not overstate automatic CBA permission.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in casebook Notes; full court opinion not reproduced

entries.title: CBA executive orders ordinarily not privately judicially enforceable
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: EO 12866 § 10 disclaims private judicial rights; failure to comply with OIRA CBA generally alone does not invalidate rule, although analyses in record can matter under § 706 reasonableness review.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even a sloppy White House economic worksheet might not give you a separate lawsuit—but if agency relies on false numbers, court can assess reasoning.
entries.legalExplanation: Judge evaluates actual factual basis as part of rule's substantive legality, distinct from action to enforce presidential order.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether challenge grounded in statute/APA arbitrary/capricious or only EO itself.
entries.examTrap: No private cause of action does not shield all relied-on CBA from review.

entries.title: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act review limits
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: UMRA directs certain large-cost regulations to include cost-benefit statement, but courts cannot vacate rules merely because statement omitted or inadequate (textbook example).
entries.laymanExplanation: A law may demand paperwork but give weak judicial remedies for omissions.
entries.legalExplanation: 2 U.S.C. §§ 1532 and 1571 govern limited court relief.
entries.examApplication: Check statute-specific remedy, not just duty.
entries.examTrap: No automatic vacatur.

entries.title: NEPA and RFA specialized analysis
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: NEPA requires environmental impact statements for major federal actions significantly affecting environment; RFA requires small-entity impacts analysis; SBREFA 1996 made RFA violations reviewable.
entries.laymanExplanation: One analysis asks environmental harms; another asks how rules affect small businesses.
entries.legalExplanation: Distinct thresholds and judicial-review provisions; RFA isn't only about most expensive rules.
entries.examApplication: Classify which analysis statute applies and how courts can enforce it.
entries.examTrap: Don't confuse RFA with full formal CBA for every rule.

entries.title: SEC efficiency, competition, capital formation test
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: D.C. Circuit reads SEC statutory duty to consider efficiency, competition and capital formation to demand rigorous economic analysis in certain financial rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency regulating markets must evaluate regulatory effects where Congress commands.
entries.legalExplanation: Business Roundtable v SEC is cited as economic reason-giving precedent; actual statute is source of obligation.
entries.examApplication: Quote mandate and map deficient calculations.
entries.examTrap: Not proof all agencies must perform Business Roundtable style CBA.

topics.title: § 5.8.2 — Corrosion Proof Fittings, TSCA and Regulatory Ossification (pp. 335–340)
topics.description: Full Fifth Circuit case excerpt, old least burdensome statute, quantification issues, historical post-2016 law and discounting.

entries.title: Corrosion Proof Fittings v. EPA, 947 F.2d 1201 (5th Cir. 1991)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Mostly no. Fifth Circuit remanded main ban provisions, retaining minor rules for products no longer sold. EPA failed to quantify intermediate less burdensome alternatives, used flawed cost/benefit discounting and timing, truncated benefits horizon, possibly double counted costs, and invoked unquantified benefits too broadly.
entries.laymanExplanation: Under pre-2016 TSCA, EPA must reasonably assess material costs/benefits and genuinely evaluate intermediate least burdensome alternatives; judicial review may reject unsupported aggregate numbers and arbitrary methodology.
entries.legalExplanation: Original statute not zero-risk: required comparison of less burdensome controls, not merely full ban vs status quo. Court questioned discounting from exposure rather than delayed disease manifestation and asymmetric discount treatment, neglect of beyond-2000 lifetime benefits, and costly product-specific lives saved. Later law changed significantly in 2016 and EPA adopted new asbestos regulation in 2024 (as textbook reports), so historical decision does not represent unchanged current TSCA mandate.
entries.examApplication: Separate old statute from amended modern TSCA; examine 3 options (no ban/intermediate/full), time horizon, discounting, double count and statistical lives.
entries.examTrap: Never claim post-2016 EPA must still satisfy identical old TSCA least-burdensome text; court did not deny asbestos can cause serious harm.
entries.sourceRole: Excerpt of judicial opinion reproduced in uploaded textbook
entries.facts: EPA adopted extensive ban on asbestos manufacturing/import/use based on health harms from mesothelioma/asbestosis/cancer. Original TSCA §6(a) required regulating 'unreasonable risk' by 'least burdensome requirements.' EPA assessed total ban versus no ban, projected 148 or 202 lives saved and cost $450–800m, while calculations varied by product and horizon.
entries.issue: Did EPA show that nearly total asbestos ban satisfied old TSCA duty to weigh impacts, analyze alternatives, and impose least-burdensome rule necessary to protect from unreasonable risk?
entries.holding: Mostly no. Fifth Circuit remanded main ban provisions, retaining minor rules for products no longer sold. EPA failed to quantify intermediate less burdensome alternatives, used flawed cost/benefit discounting and timing, truncated benefits horizon, possibly double counted costs, and invoked unquantified benefits too broadly.
entries.reasoning: Original statute not zero-risk: required comparison of less burdensome controls, not merely full ban vs status quo. Court questioned discounting from exposure rather than delayed disease manifestation and asymmetric discount treatment, neglect of beyond-2000 lifetime benefits, and costly product-specific lives saved. Later law changed significantly in 2016 and EPA adopted new asbestos regulation in 2024 (as textbook reports), so historical decision does not represent unchanged current TSCA mandate.
entries.rule: Under pre-2016 TSCA, EPA must reasonably assess material costs/benefits and genuinely evaluate intermediate least burdensome alternatives; judicial review may reject unsupported aggregate numbers and arbitrary methodology.

entries.title: Old TSCA 'least burdensome' demanded meaningful intermediate alternatives
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: EPA had to study feasible intermediate restrictions instead of assuming only no regulation or total ban.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government might demand protective masks or partial restrictions rather than automatically banning every asbestos item.
entries.legalExplanation: Casebook says merely mentioning alternatives was insufficient under then-current statutory phrasing.
entries.examApplication: List realistic intermediate technologies, phased bans and data costs.
entries.examTrap: 2016 TSCA amendment altered the controlling framework.

entries.title: Corrosion Proof: apples-to-apples discounting
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court disapproved discounting monetary costs without equivalent handling of benefits and criticized using initial asbestos exposure date rather than date harm actually materialized.
entries.laymanExplanation: Late cancer should be counted on the year cancer manifests, not falsely treated as instant harm at exposure for the discount clock.
entries.legalExplanation: Proper comparable time horizon/rates matter when burdens now and benefits much later.
entries.examApplication: For calculations show PV = amount/(1+r)^t and specify start of t.
entries.examTrap: The court's philosophical position on discounting lives is controversial in notes.

entries.title: Court's product-specific cost per life examples
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Asbestos pipe ban projected 3 lives saved at $128–227m cost, or about $42.7–75.7m/life; shingles 0.32 lives at $23–34m, about $71.9–106.3m/life. These illustrate court's concerns.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some specific product bans looked extremely costly per estimated life saved.
entries.legalExplanation: The dissenting textbook notes point out aggregate ban might look much more cost-effective; choice of denominator matters.
entries.examApplication: Show numerator cost and denominator statistical lives, not deaths as discrete individuals.
entries.examTrap: Do not call these current VSL thresholds or permanent EPA valuation rules.

entries.title: Aggregate casebook counter-calculation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Total ban cost $450–800m and projected 148–202 lives saved yields approximate range $2.23m/life (450/202) to $5.41m/life (800/148), depending on endpoints. Notes question product-specific selection.
entries.laymanExplanation: Looking at whole rule can look cheaper per life saved than isolating its worst parts.
entries.legalExplanation: Aggregation may hide unjustified subcomponents, while isolated examples may hide broad gain; both viewpoints are for analysis.
entries.examApplication: Compute ranges but leave comparative normative question unresolved.

entries.title: Unquantified benefits cannot do all the work under old TSCA
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court allowed unquantified lives beyond agency's 13-year horizon potentially tip close cases but not rescue huge unexplained negative calculation.
entries.laymanExplanation: You cannot ignore future lives in spreadsheet, then invoke them vaguely to justify any price.
entries.legalExplanation: Later-onset disease makes limited horizon especially consequential; court viewed insufficient measurement as fatal to review.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether benefits genuinely impossible to quantify, explain limitations and missing time horizon.
entries.examTrap: Critics argue court's demands ossified TSCA toxic regulation.

entries.title: TSCA 2016 revision changed significance of Corrosion Proof
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Congress relaxed old constraints via Lautenberg Act in 2016; textbook states EPA finalized new asbestos ban 2024 after decades without much §6(a) regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: The decision shaped history, but Congress later rewrote what EPA must prove.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate historical pre-2016 rule and later enactment, without claiming modern legal detail not in source.
entries.examApplication: Exam distinguish old statute literal 'least burdensome' from current amended text.
entries.examTrap: The casebook uses historical comparison; do not apply old rule as current statutory requirement.

entries.title: Ossification: overly rigorous review can freeze rules
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Critics say Corrosion Proof Fittings' demands for near-perfect CBA made hazardous chemical regulation impracticable; others say statute demanded hard balancing.
entries.laymanExplanation: If proof burden too hard, agency stops regulating even real harms.
entries.legalExplanation: Book reports EPA regulated very few existing toxic substances under old §6(a), despite alternatives and later reform.
entries.examApplication: Weigh rule-of-law statutory text versus public health administrative capacity.

topics.title: § 5.8.3 — State Regulatory Analysis: Mandates, Limits and Cell Phone Proposal (pp. 340–344)
topics.description: State resource burden, California and Texas experience, thresholds, small-business impact statements and assigned cell-phone legislative drafting hypothetical.

entries.title: State analysis mandates often operate on limited funds
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: States commonly require some regulatory impact statements but agencies may lack trained economists and funding; intensity varies and rigorous analyses may burden small offices.
entries.laymanExplanation: Big federal-style CBA may be too expensive for a tiny state licensing board.
entries.legalExplanation: Book cites 52 Experiments comparative study and skeptical response; tradeoffs of administrative capacity and statistical analysis.
entries.examApplication: Identify actual state APA trigger and agency resources.
entries.examTrap: Don't infer all states must meet federal EO 12866 thresholds.

entries.title: California elaborate process tradeoffs
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: California has complex rulemaking findings and impact statements; ABA critique says slow lawyer-intensive process yields boilerplate, litigation leverage and reduced regulatory output.
entries.laymanExplanation: More paperwork can mean fewer important health or safety rules actually issued.
entries.legalExplanation: A policy criticism of procedural burden, not blanket invalidation of California system.
entries.examApplication: Compare transparency/accuracy gains with costs of rules delayed.
entries.examTrap: Policy debate should not be substituted for state statute.

entries.title: State CBA thresholds and 2010 MSAPA § 305(a)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: 2010 model recommends analysis for rules above economic-impact amount that each enacting state must fill; threshold should be proportional to agency capabilities.
entries.laymanExplanation: State lawmakers choose how large a rule must be before mandatory study starts.
entries.legalExplanation: Unlike statutory blank, some states require impact review for all regulations; courts vary in depth of review.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether proposed rule satisfies state dollar-cost or significant impact trigger.
entries.examTrap: No universal mandatory dollar number in model provision.

entries.title: State courts may review analysis deferentially
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Some states accept general qualitative assessments without exact dollar figures; Methodist Hospitals upheld somewhat vague yearly benefits/costs statement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency may satisfy law by describing costs even without calculating every dollar if statute allows.
entries.legalExplanation: Yet Texas Unified Loans required documented evidence of no small-business impact and contemporaneous publication for comment.
entries.examApplication: Compare law wording, actual data, and substantial compliance.
entries.examTrap: Not every cost-benefit statement error invalidates regulation.

entries.title: Unified Loans v. Pettijohn, 955 S.W.2d 649 (Tex. App. 1997)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Pawnshop rules' small-business impact statement unsupported; state law required analysis where adverse effects possible and publication with NPRM.
entries.laymanExplanation: Small firm burden cannot be waved away without data.
entries.legalExplanation: Court rejected reading 'adverse impact' to mean disproportionate harm over large firms.
entries.examApplication: Analyze actual statutory trigger.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in casebook Notes; full court opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Methodist Hospitals v. Texas Industrial Accident Board, 798 S.W.2d 651 (Tex. App. 1990)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court accepted relatively general qualitative benefit-cost note for state hospital reimbursement regulation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts sometimes grant considerable leeway in cost statements.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast Unified Loans demand for evidence.
entries.sourceRole: Case discussed in casebook Notes; full court opinion not reproduced

entries.title: Designing a state analysis mandate: legislative choices
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Legislator must decide trigger, technical capacity, substantive benefit-cost criterion, treatment of distribution/unquantified effects, judicial review and remedies; blanket EO 12866 incorporation may not fit state statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before importing a federal model, ask: who pays for analysts, how to value lives, and what court may do with bad study?
entries.legalExplanation: Madison cell-phone problem tests whether law already requires CBA, whether benefit must exceed cost, and good-faith procedural review.
entries.examApplication: Treat each proposed statutory subsection (a), (b), (c) separately.
entries.examTrap: No ordinary APA requirement automatically imposes full mandatory formal CBA.

problems.title: Sunstein versus Heinzerling & Ackerman
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 325–329)
problems.prompt: Compare competing arguments about monetizing deaths, public health, discounting, opportunity costs, distribution and transparency. Which perspective works best for mandatory regulation?

problems.title: Numerical drill: benefit range
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 325–327)
problems.prompt: Using the casebook's illustration of 20 prevented deaths at $3–8m each plus $40m other gains against $200m cost, calculate low/high benefit and net benefit; practice without recording answer in problem.

problems.title: Discounting choices and health outcomes
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 328–329)
problems.prompt: What changes when benefits occur decades after exposures? Discuss different discount rates, time of exposure versus manifestation, and arguments against using present-value approach for lives.

problems.title: Executive order vs organic statute
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 330–334)
problems.prompt: When a federal agency's rule is supported by OIRA CBA but congressional statute uses 'maximum feasible' language, does executive analysis displace statutory test? Compare Cotton Dust, Michigan, Entergy.

problems.title: What judicial remedy for bad CBA?
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 332–334)
problems.prompt: Differentiate failure to follow EO 12866, RFA as amended by SBREFA, UMRA and organic statute explicitly requiring cost consideration. Analyze why private review varies.

problems.title: NHTSA light truck CAFE / Smart Energy Coalition — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 334–335)
problems.prompt: NHTSA increased light truck CAFE standards less than environmentalists wanted, using OIRA-approved CBA monetizing fuel, technology and crash/noise effects but excluding carbon emission climate benefits as beyond statutory authority/diffuse. EPCA directs 'maximum feasible' fuel efficiency considering technology, economy, other rules, conservation need. Coalition challenges use of CBA and failure to include climate change. Analyze statutory authorization, missing benefits, arbitrary/capricious and EO limits without solving.

problems.title: Statutory and methodological flaws in asbestos ban
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 335–338)
problems.prompt: List all independent reasons court rejected EPA's original asbestos ban, including least-burdensome alternatives, discounting, time horizon and double counting, without making this a solved problem.

problems.title: Product-by-product versus aggregate valuation
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 338–339)
problems.prompt: Calculate aggregate approximate cost per life versus court's high product-specific costs. Does one approach better reflect TSCA least-burdensome test?

problems.title: Discount future disease benefits
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 338–339)
problems.prompt: Should asbestos morbidity prevented decades later be valued using discount rate from exposure date or disease manifestation, if at all? Explain consistency and intergenerational debate.

problems.title: State regulatory analysis tradeoffs
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 340–343)
problems.prompt: Why might a state omit or limit CBA mandates? Compare economic expertise, budgets, threshold and litigation risk, California's elaborate system and benefits of transparency.

problems.title: State small-business impact statements
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 343)
problems.prompt: A state officer asserts pawnshop safety standards cost small businesses nothing without record evidence. Under model and Texas-style statutory mandates what must be shown?

problems.title: Madison MTD handheld-phone bill / KIT — major textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 5, pp. 324–344 (uploaded Nov. 24, 2026) (p. 343–344)
problems.prompt: Madison MTD proposed handheld phone driver ban under authority to adopt reasonable vehicle safety measures; KIT submitted Grace study alleging hands-free risk same and enforcement expensive. Rep Larry proposes law (a) require EO 12866-style analysis for significant MTD rules, (b) forbid rule unless benefits commensurate with costs, (c) allow court set aside for lack of good faith effort. Advise legislative amendments, whether CBA already required and value/risk of judicial review—leave questions unanswered.
